idiom_name: encapsulated class (private setters, backing fields) persisted by EF Core
implementation_notes: A rich entity is an ordinary class: private setters, command methods and read-only collection views over private backing fields; EF Core persists it because it materialises through a (possibly private) parameterless constructor, writes properties through their backing fields, and accepts field-only mappings when a property should not be exposed at all. Configure encapsulated collections with PropertyAccessMode.Field and keep all mapping (owned types, value converters, table names) in IEntityTypeConfiguration classes outside the entity. Value objects become records or record structs with value equality.
pitfalls: Exposing ICollection<T> - or a settable collection property - lets callers and serializers add lines without the domain method; expose a read-only view over the private field and map it with PropertyAccessMode.Field.
A public parameterless constructor plus public setters makes it easy to materialise an entity in an illegal state; keep the EF constructor private or protected.
A store-generated key must remain writable by EF (a private setter is enough); a truly read-only key field requires explicit field mapping.

variants.name: Persistence-ignorant POCOs with external mapping
variants.idiom_name: domain POCOs + IEntityTypeConfiguration/mappers outside the model
variants.implementation_notes: The domain project references no persistence package: entities are plain C# classes (or records for immutable concepts) with domain methods, and mapping is expressed in a separate infrastructure assembly through IEntityTypeConfiguration, value converters and owned types. Choose it when the model deliberately differs from the schema, when several bounded contexts share the entity types, or when the domain must stay testable without EF Core types. The trade-off is a second place that must be kept in step with the model.
pitfalls: Without the annotation-based guardrails, mapping drift goes unnoticed: keep an integration test that round-trips each aggregate through the database.
Read-only properties and collections are not mapped by convention; configure the field explicitly or EF Core will not see the collection.
Splitting model and mapping doubles the places to change when the domain evolves - only worth it when the model genuinely differs from the schema.
